title: St. Patricks Day

jokes.text: Wake up, mother-. / Die, demon! / Why didn't you ever call me back?
jokes.setup: Jack lists the disasters from Tracy and Jenna hosting the St. Patrick's Day parade in prior years, with increasingly alarming flashback snippets.
jokes.punchline: The third clip — 'Why didn't you ever call me back?' — subverts the pattern of violence/chaos with a mundane romantic complaint, making it absurdly out of place.
jokes.explanation: Classic rule of three with a misdirection payoff. First two clips follow an expected pattern (chaos, violence), the third pivots to something banal and romantic. Efficient, well-structured cold-open joke.

jokes.text: Unfortunately, unless Harry's Law really took off this week and no one told me, you two are the biggest stars at the network.
jokes.setup: Jack needs to explain why Tracy and Jenna are being trusted with the parade despite their history
jokes.punchline: The dismissive aside about 'Harry's Law' signals that it's a terrible, low-rated show — the joke is in the condescension and the very specific pop-culture put-down
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry-insider joke. Jack's disdain is perfectly in character — he's dismissing a real NBC show as a joke. The 'and no one told me' construction is a nice flourish of Jack's obliviousness to anything beneath him. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I'll take care of Tracy and Jenna like they're my own children. Which is a bad example, because I left my kids at a Sears in 2004.
jokes.setup: Hazel reassures Kenneth she'll care for Tracy and Jenna like her own children — a warm, responsible-sounding promise.
jokes.punchline: She immediately undercuts it by admitting she abandoned her actual children at a Sears in 2004.
jokes.explanation: Hazel is established as a cheerfully unhinged character, and this joke perfectly encapsulates that in one tight construction. The specificity of 'Sears' and '2004' elevates it above a generic 'bad mom' joke. The setup sounds sincere, making the pivot hit hard. Among the episode's best constructed one-liners.

jokes.text: He's only allergic to allergy medication. But he loves it.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is briefing Hazel on Tracy's allergies in a serious, professional manner.
jokes.punchline: Tracy is allergic specifically to the cure for allergies — and is addicted to it.
jokes.explanation: A compact absurdist gag that's entirely consistent with Tracy as a character. The 'but he loves it' kicker is perfectly timed and adds a tragic-comedic second layer. Efficient and character-specific.

jokes.text: The U.S. Rodeo Association does not lift lifetime bans.
jokes.setup: Hazel says 'This is my rodeo now' and then immediately clarifies 'Well, not literally, of course.'
jokes.punchline: The clarification reveals she has a genuine lifetime ban from the U.S. Rodeo Association — a wildly specific absurd backstory delivered offhand.
jokes.explanation: Another rapid-fire Hazel backstory joke. The specificity — a lifetime ban from rodeo — makes a throwaway line feel like a deep character revelation. Economy is excellent; it's a one-sentence dark joke that implies a universe of chaos.

jokes.text: Don't you want to celebrate Ireland's great accomplishments, like Michael Lohan and vomiting into a bagpipe?
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz if she'll celebrate St. Patrick's Day.
jokes.punchline: He frames Ireland's 'great accomplishments' as Michael Lohan (famously disreputable) and vomiting into a bagpipe.
jokes.explanation: Michael Lohan is a topical celebrity reference (effective in 2012), and the 'vomiting into a bagpipe' image is vivid and absurd. Slightly dated now but structurally sound. Jack's patrician condescension toward the Irish fits his character.

jokes.text: I will be wearing head-to-toe orange, in honor of Protestant William of Orange, inventor of the Orange, according to Yahoo Answers.
jokes.setup: Liz refuses to wear green for St. Patrick's Day and explains her deliberate protest.
jokes.punchline: Her historically-adjacent defiance is undercut by sourcing her facts from Yahoo Answers — implying William of Orange did not, in fact, invent the orange.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's standout jokes. It does multiple things simultaneously: (1) establishes Liz's contrarian nerd personality perfectly, (2) has a real historical kernel (William of Orange IS real), (3) the 'according to Yahoo Answers' kicker implies she half-knows she's on shaky ground but commits anyway. The specificity — not just 'the internet' but Yahoo Answers — is inspired. Could only come from Liz Lemon.

jokes.text: Criss and I are going to ride out hurricane shamrock holed up in my apartment, laughing at excerpts from Angela's Ashes.
jokes.setup: Liz describes her anti-St. Patrick's Day plans.
jokes.punchline: 'Hurricane Shamrock' is a perfect coinage for her disdain, and laughing at Angela's Ashes (a notoriously bleak Irish memoir) flips the reverential treatment of Irish suffering.
jokes.explanation: 'Hurricane Shamrock' is a great original coinage. Using Angela's Ashes as ironic anti-Irish entertainment is darkly funny. Classic Liz Lemon voice — overthought, specific, and slightly mean.

jokes.text: Oh, what are they going to do about it, write a meandering play about how amazing the Irish are at not overcoming adversity?
jokes.setup: Jack warns that some people might find Liz's anti-Irish-holiday attitude offensive.
jokes.punchline: Liz dismisses the Irish cultural community by insulting both their theater and their historical narrative of suffering-as-identity.
jokes.explanation: 'Not overcoming adversity' is a sharp reversal — Irish culture fetishizes resilience-through-suffering, and calling it out as failure to overcome is a genuinely clever inversion. 'Meandering play' is less sharp but earns its place.

jokes.text: Well, I'm sorry we can't all belong to ethnic groups as beloved as the Germans. Please, without Germans, you wouldn't have any of the Indiana Jones movies.
jokes.setup: Jack sarcastically defends his German heritage against Liz's dismissiveness.
jokes.punchline: His defense of Germans rests on the Indiana Jones movies — in which Germans are the villains.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. Jack's patrician obliviousness is the engine — he sincerely believes Germans deserve credit for Indiana Jones, apparently unaware (or unconcerned) they are the antagonists. The logic is airtight within Jack's worldview: without villains, no movies. The joke works on two levels simultaneously and is entirely character-specific. A genuine standout.

jokes.text: After all, I am your mentor, you dated Dennis Duffy, and in the '90s, you gave money to the IRA. / I thought it was contributing to a retirement account.
jokes.setup: Jack is proving that Liz secretly loves the Irish by listing evidence.
jokes.punchline: Liz donated to the IRA (Irish Republican Army) thinking it was an Individual Retirement Account — a perfect Liz Lemon financial/political naivety joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The IRA/IRA homonym is a pun but it's earned by being deeply character-specific — it's exactly the kind of mistake Liz Lemon would make. It also implies she was both financially unsophisticated AND inadvertently a terrorist sympathizer, which is a perfect Liz Lemon catastrophe. The deadpan delivery of 'I thought it was contributing to a retirement account' is pitch-perfect.

jokes.text: What is that? A curse? Take it back, you witch!
jokes.setup: Jack says 'I think someone needs to learn a St. Patrick's Day lesson' — a benign, mentor-y statement.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately panics that it's a literal supernatural curse and calls Jack a witch.
jokes.explanation: Sets up the episode's curse plot. Liz's paranoid overreaction is funny and in character. Not the sharpest joke but functional as a scene-closer and plot-setter.

jokes.text: This American Life, Saturday, March 17th... Hey, what are you doing? Get out of my studio! Happy St. Patrick's day! Let go of me! Didn't you hear my show on bullying?
jokes.setup: Liz has apparently set up a replica of the This American Life studio in her apartment to play ambient radio noise.
jokes.punchline: The host on the radio is being physically attacked by St. Patrick's Day revelers in his own studio, breaking the dignified TAL facade.
jokes.explanation: 'Didn't you hear my show on bullying?' is a genuinely funny line — the NPR host invoking his own programming while being assaulted is a perfect piece of absurdist media satire. Quick and punchy.

jokes.text: Look at them spin around. They're so confused. It's too many Megans, right?
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are watching something out the window.
jokes.punchline: They've apparently been shouting 'Megan' into the street and watching drunk parade-goers spin around confused because many of them respond to the name.
jokes.explanation: A simple but effective visual gag about a generationally common name. The couple's amusement at this petty prank is charming and funny. 'Too many Megans' is an unexpectedly sharp observation about millennial name patterns.

jokes.text: I just ordered thai food. How much do you love me now?
jokes.setup: Criss says 'I love you' and Liz responds 'Uh huh' — notably NOT saying it back.
jokes.punchline: Criss immediately tries to earn the 'I love you' back by announcing he ordered Thai food — a small but telling joke about the relationship dynamic and Liz's emotional unavailability.
jokes.explanation: This joke does double duty: it's funny on its face (bribing someone with takeout to say 'I love you') AND it plants the episode's emotional throughline about Liz's inability to say 'I love you.' The setup is the 'Uh huh' non-response. Earns rewatch bonus because the payoff at the end recontextualizes this moment.

jokes.text: You know what, I can't wait till the Asians take over. Thank God for delivery, keeping us inside and safe from all the Irish nonsense.
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are hiding inside watching the chaos.
jokes.punchline: Liz's xenophobia-inversion joke — she's not 'afraid' of Asians taking over, she's enthusiastically looking forward to it because of efficient delivery services.
jokes.explanation: A joke that plays on stereotype inversion — using a xenophobic trope but subverting the expected negativity into enthusiasm. Slightly risky humor, and the 'delivery' connection is clever but not exceptional. Functional.

jokes.text: I tried to steal beer from a Duane Reade, and some black guy cold-cocked me. / Ooh, like a security guard? / I don't know, pal. I don't see people that way.
jokes.setup: Dennis explains how he got a concussion on St. Patrick's Day.
jokes.punchline: Criss asks if it was a security guard (implying he sees the person's race as meaningful context). Dennis claims to be colorblind — which is satirically undercut by the fact that he mentioned the race unprompted.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical joke about a certain type of casual racism masquerading as 'not seeing color.' Dennis introduced race into the story himself, then performs progressive colorblindness. The irony is airtight, character-specific, and lands cleanly. Criss's straight-man clarifying question is perfectly set up.

jokes.text: Oh, Michael Jackson's ghost... / Oh, Great Kabbalah monster...
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna agree to pray together before going on air.
jokes.punchline: Each begins a prayer to their own absurdist deity — Tracy to Michael Jackson's ghost, Jenna to the 'Great Kabbalah Monster.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect character joke for both Tracy and Jenna. Tracy's reverence for Michael Jackson is a running character trait; Jenna's Kabbalah Monster is absurdist celebrity-religion satire. The simultaneous parallel prayers is a great visual. Tight and character-specific.

jokes.text: NBC is showing the promo I worked on for the parade! I'm famous.
jokes.setup: Hazel is watching TV backstage.
jokes.punchline: Hazel believes seeing a promo she worked on constitutes her being 'famous' — conflating behind-the-scenes work with celebrity.
jokes.explanation: A decent character beat for Hazel establishing her outsized ambition. Not a sharp joke structurally, more of a character reveal. Gets the job done.

jokes.text: They said my name first. / But I'm more famous than you.
jokes.setup: The NBC promo lists the parade hosts as 'Jenna Maroney and Tracy Jordan.'
jokes.punchline: This immediately triggers a billing war between Tracy and Jenna, each convinced they're the bigger star — the central Tracy/Jenna conflict of the episode.
jokes.explanation: The billing dispute is a classic sitcom premise that fits these characters perfectly. Not a sharp joke on its own but effectively plants the Tracy/Jenna plot engine for the episode.

jokes.text: Like on the set of Ocean's 12, when I put that snake in George Clooney's bed. I was not in the movie.
jokes.setup: Tracy compares the billing situation to a 'Hollywood prank.'
jokes.punchline: He put a snake in George Clooney's bed while NOT being in the movie — an uninvited onset trespasser who pranked a star.
jokes.explanation: The 'I was not in the movie' tag is what makes this. Tracy infiltrated a major Hollywood production to prank a star and somehow this is presented as a normal anecdote. Entirely consistent with Tracy's unhinged world-without-consequences existence.

jokes.text: I'll replace your lizard with a gay guy in a giant champagne bottle.
jokes.setup: Jenna is escalating threats in the dressing room fight with Tracy.
jokes.punchline: The threat is so bizarre and specific — replacing a pet lizard with a gay man inside a champagne bottle — that it becomes pure absurdist comedy.
jokes.explanation: Peak Jenna absurdism. The image is so specific and bizarre that it earns a genuine laugh. 'Gay guy in a giant champagne bottle' implies a whole backstory: how does Jenna have access to this? Why is this her go-to threat? The joke trusts the audience to find the specificity funny without explaining it.

jokes.text: Siri, kill Jenna!
jokes.setup: Tracy is furious at Jenna in the dressing room escalation.
jokes.punchline: He tries to use Apple's Siri voice assistant to murder his coworker.
jokes.explanation: A very economical joke — three words that perfectly blend Tracy's worldview (technology should obey him) with absurdism. The timely Siri reference works in context (2012) but slightly cheaper because it's a tech name-drop. Still, it's genuinely funny and quotable.

jokes.text: I get second billing to this small-boobied grandma?
jokes.setup: Tracy is furious about the billing.
jokes.punchline: His insult of Jenna is gendered and ageist in a way that's startlingly specific and crude, which is funny as a character beat.
jokes.explanation: A relatively cheap insult joke. Tracy's crudeness is character-consistent but the joke relies on the insult itself being funny rather than any clever construction. Functional but lower craft.

jokes.text: The only baloney Tracy has is the baloney he's full of.
jokes.setup: Jack tries to invoke their 'My Baloney' secret handshake to remind them of their friendship.
jokes.punchline: Jenna repurposes 'baloney' as an insult — he's full of BS — abandoning the handshake's meaning.
jokes.explanation: A callback to 'My baloney' that works as a wordplay pivot. It's clever enough — using the callback word against Tracy — but not exceptional. The double meaning of 'baloney' (the food vs. nonsense) is functional wordplay.

jokes.text: Jenna thinks that Christina Aguilera lost her voice during childbirth.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining to Hazel why they don't let Tracy and Jenna watch NBC.
jokes.punchline: Jenna holds a surreally wrong celebrity belief — she thinks Christina Aguilera, famous for a powerful voice, lost it during childbirth.
jokes.explanation: A great detail about Jenna's insane internal world. It's not just that Jenna has wrong celebrity info; it's that she's built a whole alternate reality where Christina Aguilera had a voice and lost it to childbirth. The specificity makes it funny.

jokes.text: I don't like the way you're talking to me. Why don't we drive to Sears? I'll buy you a toy.
jokes.setup: Hazel is annoyed at being lectured by Jack.
jokes.punchline: She offers to take Jack to Sears and buy him a toy — a callback to her abandoned children at Sears, now redeployed as a condescending threat.
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback that darkens the original joke retroactively — going to Sears with Hazel is ominous, not reassuring. The callback is earned and tight. Hazel using her child abandonment history as a threat is disturbing and funny.

jokes.text: None of the writers can go out on St. Patrick's day because we all have faces people naturally just want to punch.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Frank what the writers are doing on a Saturday.
jokes.punchline: Frank explains with blunt self-awareness that their collective punchable faces force them to stay indoors on a day when drunk people have lowered inhibitions.
jokes.explanation: Self-aware comedy about comedy writers' appearance. The logic is absurd but perfectly coherent within the show's world. 'Faces people naturally just want to punch' is a memorable phrase. Strong economy, strong character integration for the writer characters.

jokes.text: Colonizers of Malaar. It's a strategy board game from the makers of Goblet Quest and Virginity Keep.
jokes.setup: Frank introduces the board game the writers are playing.
jokes.punchline: The game is a Settlers of Catan parody, but the companion titles — 'Goblet Quest' and 'Virginity Keep' — perfectly sketch the nerd-culture audience without a word of explanation.
jokes.explanation: 'Virginity Keep' is inspired — a game where you protect your virginity, perfectly targeting the nerd-gamer stereotype. 'Goblet Quest' is a nice additional absurdist detail. Good economy: the two titles do enormous character work.

jokes.text: You have a monopoly on wheat. But what happens if you overproduce, flood the markets? Prices drop, your economy collapses. You've got to diversify, Frank. It's basic capitalism.
jokes.setup: Jack, a titan of industry, stumbles onto a fantasy board game in the writers' room.
jokes.punchline: He immediately applies real corporate strategy to a fantasy board game, unable to switch off his CEO brain.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-comedy. The joke is that Jack cannot engage with anything — even a fantasy board game — without applying ruthless capitalist logic. The parallel structure (wheat/commodity economics) means his advice is both correct AND insane. High character integration: only Jack Donaghy does this.

jokes.text: Uh, unicorns? / Can you breed and sell them? There's got to be a market for unicorns. If I've learned anything from reading Liddy's princess books, unicorn hair has magical properties. You've got to know your product, Frank.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Frank what resources he has in the game besides wheat.
jokes.punchline: Jack pivots seamlessly from real economics to unicorn market analysis, citing his daughter's princess books as research — never breaking his serious CEO demeanor.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from commodity economics to unicorn market analysis is perfect. The detail 'from reading Liddy's princess books' humanizes Jack while making the absurdity more grounded. 'Unicorn hair has magical properties' delivered as a genuine business insight is peak Jack Donaghy. Could only be this character.

jokes.text: 'Unicorn,' a death ray.
jokes.setup: Jack says to replace 'Malaar' with 'Fairfield, Connecticut' and 'unicorn' with '...' — implying a mundane business product.
jokes.punchline: A death ray.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke by a significant margin. It has a perfectly engineered pause — the whole speech about Fairfield, Connecticut builds the expectation of a normal corporate product. The cutaway to Jack's face, then simply 'a death ray,' delivered as though it's perfectly mundane, is sublime. The economy is unmatched: two words that reveal Jack's secret corporate agenda AND are inherently absurd. The structure (the long pause before the tag) is textbook. This is comparable to the high-end anchor examples — it's elegant, character-defining, and genuinely surprising.

jokes.text: Hot dog truck, huh? I went entrepreneur, too. I got this new business where I burn your old DVDs onto laserdisc.
jokes.setup: Dennis appears at Liz's apartment, injured, and sees Criss's hot dog truck.
jokes.punchline: His entrepreneurial venture is burning DVDs (current technology) onto laserdisc (obsolete technology from the '70s/'80s) — perfect anti-logic.
jokes.explanation: Dennis Duffy's business ventures are always perfect character jokes, and this one is outstanding. Converting forward technology to backward technology is the exact wrong direction of entrepreneurship. It's a brilliant encapsulation of Dennis's inability to understand value or progress. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: I don't have health insurance because of Obama.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to call an ambulance for Dennis's concussion.
jokes.punchline: Dennis refuses to go to a hospital, blaming Obama for his lack of health insurance — ironic since the ACA was designed to expand coverage.
jokes.explanation: Topical political humor that works because Dennis's understanding of policy is predictably backward. Character-specific to a working-class, contrarian New York guy. The irony is pointed but not deeply original.

jokes.text: I was a volunteer EMT. At Burning Man. And we agreed never to talk about that. At sunset, the cacti start to resemble people looking for hugs. It gets ugly, Liz.
jokes.setup: Criss claims EMT expertise to assess Dennis's concussion. Liz is skeptical.
jokes.punchline: His EMT experience is from Burning Man — a festival famous for drug use — and he describes a trauma involving hugging cacti at sunset.
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered joke: (1) Burning Man EMT is already absurd, (2) 'we agreed never to talk about that' implies shared trauma, (3) the cactus-as-hugger detail is a specific psychedelic imagery gag. 'It gets ugly, Liz' is a perfect understatement closer. Strong construction.

jokes.text: You know, there's some things I miss about being with you, like having somewhere to hook my SEGA up to, but this constant judgment...
jokes.setup: Dennis is reflecting on what he misses about Liz, apparently about to list romantic or personal qualities.
jokes.punchline: What he misses is access to a TV to plug his SEGA into — purely practical, entirely unromantic, perfect Dennis Duffy.
jokes.explanation: A devastating character joke. Dennis begins a sentence that sounds like it might be almost sweet — 'there's some things I miss about being with you' — and the punchline is a SEGA hookup. It's funny because: (1) it's so specific (SEGA, not even a current console), (2) it perfectly encapsulates his emotional shallowness, and (3) he pivots immediately to complaining about her. One of the episode's funniest character lines. Only Dennis Duffy says this.

jokes.text: I can't get into an ambulance. I don't have health insurance because of Obama.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to get Dennis medical help
jokes.punchline: Dennis blames Obama for his lack of health insurance (ironically, the ACA was designed to provide coverage), revealing his political confusion
jokes.explanation: Good Dennis character beat, and the political irony is there (the ACA was meant to expand coverage), but it's a fairly obvious joke in 2012. In character, functional, but not exceptional.

jokes.text: It's like sex, but your husband isn't looking at a picture of a bridge.
jokes.setup: Jenna says live TV is like sex.
jokes.punchline: Her specific qualifier — that unlike sex with her husband, live TV doesn't involve him looking at a picture of a bridge — implies something deeply wrong with her marriage, delivered completely casually.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. 'A picture of a bridge' is a perfect absurdist detail — specific enough to be surprising but vague enough to spawn imaginative horror. The joke implies Jenna's husband is sexually fixated on infrastructure and she finds this completely unremarkable. The casualness of delivery is everything. Original, character-specific, memorable, and darkly funny. Among the episode's top three.

jokes.text: Duh! After you PMS-ed about their names yesterday, I thought numbers would make everyone happy.
jokes.setup: Jack asks if Hazel changed the script to 'host number one' and 'host number two.'
jokes.punchline: Hazel's solution to the name-order dispute was to remove names entirely and use numbers — which made both Tracy and Jenna read 'host number one,' creating a new crisis.
jokes.explanation: A solid situational comedy beat. The logic of the error is clear, Hazel's confidence in a bad idea is character-consistent, and 'PMS-ed' as a verb is pointed character sarcasm. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: They're both reading host number one. / Would a third host help? I am SAG eligible, but I will only do nude stuff if there's a mirror behind me.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna are both reading 'host number one' simultaneously on live TV, creating chaos.
jokes.punchline: Hazel's solution is to add herself as a third host — with the condition that she will only do nude scenes if there's a mirror behind her.
jokes.explanation: The mirror condition is the key absurdist detail — Hazel's vanity manifests even in a live crisis. Funny and character-specific, though the 'third host' premise is a bit overworked as a joke structure.

jokes.text: I'm playing two timber and one brick to build a bridge and establish a trading post in Midgar. / That failed... And the Orcs raped everybody.
jokes.setup: The writers are deep in their fantasy board game. Lutz announces his move confidently.
jokes.punchline: His ambitious plan immediately fails catastrophically, resulting in orc-based atrocities.
jokes.explanation: The quick failure and dark consequence is funny as a comedic beat, and 'Midgar' (a Final Fantasy location) is a nice easter egg for nerds. The rape reference is played for shock comedy — works as dark escalation but is a cheap laugh.

jokes.text: Don't you see what you're doing? You're creating a real estate bubble, and the only person who'll benefit is Sue, who'll buy up all the neutral land for cents on the dollar. Thanks a lot, Klootzak.
jokes.setup: The board game bubble Jack created is spiraling.
jokes.punchline: 'Klootzak' is Dutch for 'asshole' — Jack uses a foreign-language profanity in a board game dispute, which is absurd, and also implies he's calling himself out indirectly.
jokes.explanation: 'Klootzak' is a fun absurdist touch — Jack's cosmopolitan insult vocabulary applied to a fantasy board game. Slightly inside-joke territory for those who recognize the Dutch word, but the absurdity of using it in this context is clear regardless.

jokes.text: And you would presume to wield the scepter of Thalbain? / Yes. Yes, I would.
jokes.setup: Frank challenges Jack's right to dominate the board game.
jokes.punchline: Jack's utterly sincere and confident 'Yes. Yes, I would.' — delivered as though assuming the throne of a fantasy kingdom is the most natural thing in the world for him.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'Yes. Yes, I would.' is a masterclass in comedy through character voice. Jack's absolute certainty — even about fictional kingdoms — is who he is. The pause between 'Yes.' and 'Yes, I would.' implies genuine consideration followed by deeper conviction. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Dennis Duffy is like the Terminator with cheaper sunglasses. He just keeps coming back, because his potato brain thinks he still has a chance with me.
jokes.setup: Criss asks why Liz is being so hostile about Dennis.
jokes.punchline: 'Cheaper sunglasses' is a great specific downgrade of the Terminator metaphor, and 'potato brain' is an inspired Liz-ism insult.
jokes.explanation: Two strong images: the Terminator downgrade (cheaper sunglasses suggests Dennis can't even afford to be a proper unstoppable machine) and 'potato brain' as an organic, low-tech insult. The juxtaposition of sci-fi metaphor and agricultural insult is funny. Liz's voice is clear.

jokes.text: Hey, Liz, you'll be back. / If I ever see you again, I'll kill you. / You'll be back. / Never again! / You'll be back, Liz Lemon. / You'll be back.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to throw Dennis out, echoing Terminator imagery Liz herself just invoked.
jokes.punchline: Dennis becomes a literal Terminator parody — implacably repeating 'You'll be back' against Liz's increasingly heated denials, both confirming and undermining her characterization of him.
jokes.explanation: An immediate callback that the writers wisely exploited — having Dennis actually behave like the Terminator joke Liz just made about him. The escalation of Liz's denials against Dennis's patient repetition is well-structured. The irony is that he IS exactly like she described.

jokes.text: Ugh, three again? / And your yak... has smallpox.
jokes.setup: Jack is back in the writers' room, rolling dice that keep producing bad results.
jokes.punchline: Adding insult to injury: not only does he roll badly, his yak is now infected with smallpox — a very specific medieval-ish livestock disease.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of smallpox for the yak is funny — it's the right kind of wrong ailment for a fantasy game. The 'three again' establishes the pattern of bad luck. Minor but pleasant absurdist detail.

jokes.text: Rockefeller, no! What? Dennis is here. Take back your curse. This isn't funny anymore.
jokes.setup: Liz calls Jack to complain that the 'curse' he jokingly placed is coming true.
jokes.punchline: She's genuinely convinced Dennis's arrival is supernatural punishment, and 'Take back your curse' is an earnest demand — playing the show's absurdism straight.
jokes.explanation: A functional callback that maintains the curse plotline. 'Rockefeller, no!' as a phone response to the caller is a minor fun detail. Average comedic beat — maintains the episode's absurd premise but doesn't add much.

jokes.text: Oh, really? You're cursed? Try ruling over the desert wastelands of Kroth with no spell cards.
jokes.setup: Liz complains about her curse on the phone. Jack is still playing the board game.
jokes.punchline: Jack one-ups Liz's 'real' curse with his in-game predicament, treating the board game as equally serious as her actual life crisis.
jokes.explanation: Jack's utter absorption in the board game — dismissing Liz's problems by comparing them to his fantasy land problems — is both character-true and genuinely funny. The equivalence of 'cursed in real life' vs. 'no spell cards' is a great absurdist parallel.

jokes.text: The desert of Kroth is Kabletown. I've got to get some fresh air.
jokes.setup: Jack has been failing in the board game's barren wasteland.
jokes.punchline: He has an epiphany that his fictional in-game situation mirrors his real corporate frustration — the board game has accidentally given him a business breakthrough.
jokes.explanation: The moment the episode's A-plot (Jack's corporate crisis) and B-plot (board game) converge is well-executed. The line 'The desert of Kroth is Kabletown' is a great absurdist-to-real pivot. Jack has a genuine epiphany through fantasy play — the joke is that the game is more useful to him than his actual job.

jokes.text: I should take the hot dog truck out after the parade, and sell empty buns to drunk people.
jokes.setup: Dennis suggests a business opportunity to Criss.
jokes.punchline: Selling empty buns — not hot dogs, just the bun — to inebriated people who won't notice. It's both entrepreneurially savvy and deeply scammy.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's criminal-adjacent entrepreneurship is perfectly in character. 'Empty buns to drunk people' is both a terrible idea and a weirdly logical one. The specificity (parade, drunk people, buns specifically) elevates this above a generic scammer joke.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, Criss, he's just trying to get me alone so he can start a gas leak or claim squatter's rights or hit me over the head, and when I wake up, we're on our honeymoon. At SeaWorld.
jokes.setup: Criss suggests Dennis's hot dog truck idea is reasonable.
jokes.punchline: Liz's paranoid escalation from 'gas leak' through 'squatter's rights' to 'wake up at SeaWorld on our honeymoon' is a perfect list-joke that escalates in absurdity.
jokes.explanation: An excellent escalating list joke. The genius is the path: gas leak (plausible threat) → squatter's rights (absurd legal maneuver) → wake up at honeymoon (kidnapping) → SeaWorld (why SeaWorld specifically?). The terminal specificity of 'SeaWorld' makes this. Each step in the escalation is funnier, and the final destination is perfectly absurd. Very Liz Lemon.

jokes.text: And once again, the puppet will become the puppet master. / What does that mean, 'once again'? That's not a thing.
jokes.setup: Liz announces she'll manipulate Dennis by playing along with his fake girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: Criss deflates her triumphant declaration by noting she's never successfully done this — 'once again' implies a history of victory that doesn't exist.
jokes.explanation: A sharp deflation joke. Liz is self-mythologizing in real time, and Criss simply points out the gap between her narrative and reality. 'That's not a thing' is a perfectly economical kill shot. Great straight-man work from Criss.

jokes.text: Dude, you missed the end of the lez movie. Their daughter, she goes off to college, and Mark Ruffalo, he's just gonna do his own thing with the restaurant.
jokes.setup: Criss comes to check on Liz and Dennis.
jokes.punchline: He summarizes the plot of an unspecified 'lez movie' — which apparently featured Mark Ruffalo running a restaurant — as casually as if it's the most normal thing.
jokes.explanation: Mark Ruffalo in a lesbian movie 'doing his own thing with the restaurant' is a perfect absurdist detail — unexplained and confidently delivered. The summary itself sounds like a parody of real low-stakes Showtime drama. Decent.

jokes.text: She's a card girl at kangaroo boxing matches, so she's got a body, and she's loaded. Her grandfather invented the stop sign.
jokes.setup: Dennis describes his alleged girlfriend/wife Megan.
jokes.punchline: Three escalating and equally absurd status signifiers: exotic job, invented family patent for the stop sign.
jokes.explanation: 'Her grandfather invented the stop sign' is the standout — a very specific absurdist form of wealth/prestige that sounds completely made up but is delivered with total Dennis confidence. 'Card girl at kangaroo boxing matches' establishes the universe and 'stop sign' confirms it. Excellent Dennis voice.

jokes.text: Liz realization: 'Wait, Megan is real?' followed by explaining she said 'I love you' to Dennis as a tactical bluff.
jokes.setup: Dennis reveals Megan is his wife, not a fake. Liz had already said 'I love you' to Dennis thinking she was calling his bluff.
jokes.punchline: Liz's manipulation scheme completely backfires — she's now in the position of having said 'I love you' to her ex with his new wife present.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed cringe payoff. The puppet master scheme blows up spectacularly, and the layers are good — Liz manipulated herself. The situational comedy is strong and the cringe is earned.

jokes.text: He should have said my name first. Roker should be on my side. / Why, because you both have had huge weight fluctuations?
jokes.setup: Al Roker has taken over hosting and says Tracy's name before Jenna's. Tracy thinks Roker should side with him.
jokes.punchline: Jenna asks if Tracy thinks Roker is on his side because they've both had notable weight fluctuations — a reference to both Tracy's fictional weight issues and Roker's real-life gastric bypass surgery.
jokes.explanation: A quick, sharp celebrity reference joke that works on multiple levels — it calls out Tracy's fictional weight issues and Al Roker's real-life documented weight story simultaneously. The delivery as a sincere question ('Why, because...?') rather than a taunt makes it even sharper.

jokes.text: By starting a fire and then rescuing everyone from it? And then I'm a hero and then I'm Playboy?
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Hazel how she'd be famous if she got kicked out of show business.
jokes.punchline: Hazel's plan is a multi-step scheme: commit arson → perform heroic rescue → become celebrity hero → appear in Playboy. She's thought this through.
jokes.explanation: Hazel's arson-to-Playboy pipeline is both a great joke and a perfect character reveal. The precision of the logic — fire, rescue, hero, Playboy — shows she's genuinely thought this through as a viable alternative career path. Dark, absurdist, and entirely character-specific. One of the episode's best Hazel moments.

jokes.text: I feel helpless. Impotent. / Whoa, buy me a drink first. / Sorry, we've been instructed to keep it light.
jokes.setup: Jack is confessing to a priest that he feels 'impotent' — meaning powerless.
jokes.punchline: The priest takes 'impotent' in its sexual sense and tells Jack to buy him a drink first. Then immediately apologizes because he's been told to 'keep it light.'
jokes.explanation: A wordplay joke built on the double meaning of 'impotent.' The priest's sexual interpretation is a moderately well-worn Catholic priest gag, but 'we've been instructed to keep it light' is a clever meta-joke implying network/writing notes exist in-universe. Decent construction.

jokes.text: First of all, he was born in fourth century Ireland. He might as well have been born in a grave. His only worldly possession was no snakes.
jokes.setup: The priest begins telling the story of St. Patrick to inspire Jack.
jokes.punchline: 'His only worldly possession was no snakes' — reframing the 'driving out the snakes' myth as St. Patrick's sole asset being an absence.
jokes.explanation: 'His only worldly possession was no snakes' is a genuinely brilliant joke. 'Born in a grave' is strong dark comedy, but the snake line is special — it takes the well-known St. Patrick legend and reframes it as an absence rather than an achievement. You can 'possess' nothing. The economy is extraordinary: one sentence that's simultaneously a theological joke, a poverty joke, and a logic paradox. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: By the scepter of Thalbain!
jokes.setup: Jack has a business epiphany in the cathedral, inspired by the St. Patrick story.
jokes.punchline: He exclaims his epiphany using Malaar board game terminology — 'the scepter of Thalbain' — rather than any real-world expression.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback payoff. Jack has so thoroughly internalized the board game that he uses its mythology as an exclamation of genuine insight. The priest, presumably, hears this as gibberish. It also confirms the board game is now part of Jack's actual executive thinking. Extremely tight and well-earned.

jokes.text: The first car is here for whichever one of you wants to leave first.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna have had their reconciliation moment.
jokes.punchline: Hazel immediately creates a new competition — who gets the first car — undercutting the emotional resolution.
jokes.explanation: A quick Hazel beat that demonstrates she still hasn't learned. The timing (immediately after the reconciliation) is the joke. Economical but not particularly sharp on its own.

jokes.text: Why do I keep doing this stuff? Is 70 not a good IQ?
jokes.setup: Tracy has a moment of genuine self-reflection about his impulsive behavior.
jokes.punchline: His self-analysis bottoms out at 'Is 70 not a good IQ?' — revealing he knows his IQ score and genuinely doesn't know if it's acceptable.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Tracy line. The self-reflection setup makes it seem like genuine character growth, then the punchline reveals the limits of that growth: he doesn't know if 70 is a good IQ. The sincere uncertainty is perfect. Only Tracy Jordan asks this question with complete earnestness. Highly quotable and rewatch-worthy.

jokes.text: I had to beg to take over for Andy Rooney. And it did not go well. / When I was a kid, you could get a prostitute for $5.
jokes.setup: Tracy is sharing his recent professional failures — including trying to replace Andy Rooney on 60 Minutes
jokes.punchline: His Andy Rooney impression/replacement material is apparently 'When I was a kid, you could get a prostitute for $5' — an accurate parody of Rooney's nostalgic curmudgeon style applied to something completely inappropriate
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The Andy Rooney parody is sharp — capturing his nostalgic, 'when I was a kid' cadence exactly — and applying it to prostitution pricing. It's both a precision celebrity parody and a perfect Tracy line. The buildup ('it did not go well') before the reveal is excellent structure. Very quotable, high impact.

jokes.text: A year ago, I won an Oscar. Now look at me. I had to beg to take over for Andy Rooney. And it did not go well. / When I was a kid, you could get a prostitute for $5.
jokes.setup: Tracy is reflecting on his career trajectory since winning an Oscar.
jokes.punchline: His failed replacement of Andy Rooney is revealed through the one thing he apparently said on air: 'When I was a kid, you could get a prostitute for $5.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke with perfect structure. The setup (replacing Andy Rooney on 60 Minutes) creates the expectation of a curmudgeonly opinion. 'It did not go well' is a beautiful understatement setup. Then the punchline is Tracy's actual commentary — 'When I was a kid, you could get a prostitute for $5' — which is both plausible as a Tracy utterance and a perfect parody of Rooney's 'things were better when I was young' format. The logical connection between Rooney's nostalgic complaints and Tracy's version is inspired. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: I'm scared, J-Mohr. And not just 'cause today's the day that guy that tried to kill me gets out of jail.
jokes.setup: Tracy opens up to Jenna about his fear of no longer being the biggest star
jokes.punchline: He qualifies 'I'm scared' with 'and not just because today's the day that guy who tried to kill me gets out of jail' — treating his would-be assassin's release as a routine background anxiety
jokes.explanation: The 'not just because X' construction works brilliantly here — X is someone being released from jail for attempted murder, which would be most people's primary fear, but Tracy treats it as a minor qualifying footnote. Perfect deadpan understatement through structure. Highly quotable, very strong character integration.

jokes.text: Know this, Hazel. I will always be here... For them and for you. Nothing can ever make me... / Move your car.
jokes.setup: Kenneth gives an earnest, sincere speech about always being there for Hazel and the talent.
jokes.punchline: A car horn or driver interrupts at the exact moment with 'Move your car' — collapsing his emotional declaration.
jokes.explanation: A classic sitcom interruption gag — the punchline cuts off the sincere speech. Functionally effective but not an original construction. The timing-based comedy is solid but the joke itself is a familiar type.

jokes.text: I'd like to spend my remaining gold... to purchase a fire spell. / Against whom will you be casting this spell? / Against myself. I am setting fire to my own desert.
jokes.setup: Jack has returned to the board game with a new strategy, apparently having processed his epiphany.
jokes.punchline: He's going to burn his own territory — a wildly counter-intuitive move that makes perverse economic sense.
jokes.explanation: Jack applying creative destruction to a fantasy board game — burning his own land to create glass — is a perfect payoff to his arc. The absurdity of 'against myself' is a great misdirection, and then the economic logic (turn desert to glass, corner the glass market) is both insane and coherent. Jack's conviction makes it land. Excellent character-comedy escalation.

jokes.text: I'd like to spend my remaining gold to purchase a fire spell. / And against whom will you be casting this spell? / Against myself. I am setting fire to my own desert.
jokes.setup: Jack is playing Colonizers of Malaar and announces an unusual move
jokes.punchline: He's burning his own territory — explained as a strategy to produce glass as a commodity — a move so counterintuitive it seems insane until he explains the economic logic
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jack joke — his creative destruction strategy (burning his own desert to make glass) is both genuinely clever and a perfect mirror of his corporate philosophy. The move is bizarre in the game but logical in a ruthless capitalist framework. High character integration.

jokes.text: You see, it doesn't matter if I'm on the wind-blown dunes of Kroth or in the fluorescent-lit boardrooms of 30 Rockefeller Plaza. I will create something from nothing. Today Malaar... Tomorrow Kabletown.
jokes.setup: Jack delivers a triumphant speech about creating from nothing.
jokes.punchline: 'Today Malaar... Tomorrow Kabletown' — the grandiose Napoleon-esque declaration is that he conquered a children's board game and plans to apply it to a real corporation.
jokes.explanation: A great character monologue punchline. The joke is the gap between the grandeur of the rhetoric and the absurdity of the achievement (winning a fantasy board game). 'Today Malaar, Tomorrow Kabletown' is a quotable couplet that perfectly encapsulates Jack's inability to distinguish the trivial from the important — and his absolute conviction in both.

jokes.text: Your highness, you may take your right as king. / I am a virgin... with white guys.
jokes.setup: Jack has won the board game and Frank offers Sue the traditional king's 'right' — implying droit du seigneur (a feudal sexual privilege).
jokes.punchline: Sue clarifies: she is not a virgin overall, just specifically with white guys — a very specific qualifier that both defuses and complicates the moment.
jokes.explanation: A sharp misdirection with a very specific punchline. The qualifier 'with white guys' takes a simple 'I'm a virgin' joke into unexpected territory. The delivery of a very personal fact in a completely matter-of-fact way as a board game complication is absurdly funny.

jokes.text: All right, mustard only. There you go. Enjoy your bun.
jokes.setup: Criss has taken Dennis's idea and is apparently selling empty buns from the hot dog truck.
jokes.punchline: A customer orders, and Criss serves them a bun with only mustard — confirming he's executing the 'empty bun' scam.
jokes.explanation: A quick payoff to Dennis's scam idea, made funnier because it's Criss — the presumably decent hot dog vendor — executing a con. 'Enjoy your bun' is delivered with service-industry sincerity that makes it funny. Good callback economy.

jokes.text: More importantly, I have never been with someone for longer than nine months. You and I have been together for six, so I assume something will go wrong soon. You'll tell me you believe in ghosts, or I'll reveal that I am terrible at expressing my feelings.
jokes.setup: Liz is having an emotional conversation with Criss about their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Her forecast of doom escalates from 'you believe in ghosts' (his potential flaw) to 'I'm terrible at expressing my feelings' (her acknowledged flaw) — equal weighting, completely different severity.
jokes.explanation: Character-rich comedy about Liz's relationship anxiety. The false equivalence between 'believing in ghosts' (minor) and 'terrible at expressing feelings' (the episode's actual theme) is both funny and emotionally pointed. It does serious episode work while being funny.

jokes.text: Wait, is now the time on St. Patrick's day when we talk about our feelings? / I don't understand your art, Kevin.
jokes.setup: Criss questions whether this is an appropriate moment for emotional conversation, and a random passerby reacts.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't understand your art, Kevin' — a completely non-sequitur response from a stranger to Criss's confused question, implying they overheard and are baffled.
jokes.explanation: A random absurdist line from a stranger — 'I don't understand your art, Kevin' — is funny because it implies a whole different conversation that this stranger was apparently having, while also being a deeply 30 Rock type of ambient joke. Good economy, unexplained, and confidently delivered.

jokes.text: These are the only green things I own. / More importantly, I have never been with someone for longer than nine months. You and I have been together for six, so I assume something will go wrong soon. You'll tell me you believe in ghosts, or I'll reveal that I am terrible at expressing my feelings.
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss have a serious conversation outside; Liz points to what she's wearing
jokes.punchline: Liz's longest relationship has been nine months — she has never made it to a year. Her prediction of failure scenarios ('you'll tell me you believe in ghosts') is specific and self-aware
jokes.explanation: The 'nine months' revelation is funny, and 'you'll tell me you believe in ghosts' is a perfectly chosen apocalyptic relationship scenario. This is more emotional than comedic but functions as dark character comedy — Liz's romantic failure statistics are absurd.

jokes.text: But this isn't fair to you, Chris. This is the happiest I've been in a long time, and I'm sorry that I can't just be a normal person and tell you stuff. Like, nice stuff. Like... Greeting card stuff.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to confess her feelings to Criss.
jokes.punchline: 'Greeting card stuff' — her inability to name the emotion reduces it to the category of sentiment, not the sentiment itself. Both funny and genuinely touching.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful character joke that bridges comedy and genuine emotion. 'Greeting card stuff' is the perfect Liz Lemon way of almost saying 'I love you' — she can name the category of the thing she can't say. The stammer leading to it ('nice stuff. Like...') is perfectly written.

jokes.text: I love you. / I know. / You solo-ed me.
jokes.setup: Liz finally says 'I love you.' The expected response is 'I love you too.'
jokes.punchline: Criss responds with 'I know' — a Han Solo reference — and Liz immediately calls out 'You solo-ed me,' treating the romantic milestone as a Star Wars nerd competition she lost.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of 30 Rock's finest constructed moments. Everything about it is perfect: (1) It earns its emotional weight after a full episode of Liz being unable to say 'I love you.' (2) Criss's 'I know' is both genuinely sweet (he's confident) and a nerd power-play. (3) 'You solo-ed me' is an INVENTED VERB — Liz has immediately turned the most romantic moment of the episode into a competitive Star Wars reference battle. (4) The joke does not undercut the emotion — it IS the emotion for Liz Lemon. This is the platonic ideal of 30 Rock: profound character comedy where the joke and the heart are the same thing. Highest scores in the episode, justified.

jokes.text: That is a person named Liz Lemon who just told some dude she loves him. Well, I have known her for a long time and she never said that before. It sure is rewarding as a TV viewer when someone you're interested in shows growth.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Al Roker are doing parade commentary and see Liz's moment on a monitor.
jokes.punchline: Tracy and Roker narrate Liz's emotional moment as TV commentators — 'it sure is rewarding as a TV viewer when someone you're interested in shows growth' — treating the show's own protagonist as a character they're watching.
jokes.explanation: A superb meta-comedic payoff. Tracy and Roker narrating Liz's emotional growth as television commentators is a perfect 30 Rock move — it uses the show's format (live TV coverage) to deliver self-referential commentary on its own narrative. 'Rewarding as a TV viewer' is the key line — it's both Tracy's genuine sentiment and a wink to the audience experiencing the same thing.

jokes.text: Also, TV viewers liked when in a show is a song.
jokes.setup: Tracy is commentating and offers wisdom about what TV audiences like.
jokes.punchline: His grammatically mangled observation that 'TV viewers liked when in a show is a song' — a deliberately garbled meta-statement — is immediately followed by an Irish song, proving him right.
jokes.explanation: The grammatical chaos of 'TV viewers liked when in a show is a song' is itself a joke — Tracy is describing the thing that's about to happen while barely able to articulate it. Then it immediately happens. The meta-self-awareness (30 Rock ending on a musical moment) plus Tracy's broken syntax is a great episode closer joke.

jokes.text: Also, TV viewers liked when in a show is a song. ♪Oh Danny boy, the pipes, the pipes are calling♪ ... Don't you dare fade out on me.
jokes.setup: Tracy has broken the fourth wall to address TV viewers directly
jokes.punchline: He announces that TV viewers like songs, begins singing 'Danny Boy,' and then yells at the episode for daring to fade out before he finishes
jokes.explanation: Strong meta-comedy close. Tracy's TV-viewer-pleasing logic, the St. Patrick's Day song choice, and then 'don't you dare fade out on me' as the episode does exactly that is a perfect structural joke — the show itself is the punchline. Well-constructed and a satisfying close to the episode's meta thread.

jokes.text: Don't you dare fade out on me.
jokes.setup: The Irish song begins playing as the episode closes.
jokes.punchline: Liz addresses the episode itself — 'don't you dare fade out on me' — a direct meta-address to the show's production, breaking the fourth wall completely.
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode-closing joke that's also extremely economical (six words). Liz Lemon addressing the fade-out directly is a beautiful meta-comedic button — she's lived through the episode's emotional arc and now resists its conclusion. It's funny, slightly melancholy, and quintessentially 30 Rock. The gap between Liz wanting the moment to continue and the inevitable fade is the comedy.

tmdb_overview: Jack feels unworthy of his latest award and attempts to redeem himself by taking on the writers in a strategic board game. Liz believes she's cursed on St. Patrick's Day when her ex-boyfriend Dennis shows up to derail her relationship with Criss. Meanwhile, Hazel struggles to keep the peace between Tracy and Jenna.
insight: St. Patrick's Day episode hits 90.6 with 3.11 jokes per minute across 78 gags.
